stories.title: Budget to support those 'who get up early every morning'
stories.summary: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris has said this year's Budget will support people "who get up early every morning and go to work". Addressing a Mullingar Chamber of Commerce pre-Budget breakfast briefing, Mr Harris said that "if you work hard, you should be able to get ahead, not just get by". He said strong towns and strong communities across the country depend on people "who are prepared to work hard in order to get ahead". The Tánaiste also said there will be a business package that will make progress on reducing the cost base for business owners while also "increasing your ability to make ends meet". He said cutting business taxes and cutting income tax "are the priorities" as budget negotiations enter their final stage. Earlier, Social Justice Ireland's (SJI) Research and Policy Analyst Michelle Murphy said tax credits are the fairest way to deliver any income tax package in next month's Budget.

stories.title: Taoiseach to address global issues with Trump in Dublin
stories.summary: The meeting between the Taoiseach and the US President in Dublin next Saturday will address global issues according to the Minister for Public Expenditure. Jack Chambers said the meeting planned for Farmleigh House in the Phoenix Park would look at the two-way relationship between Ireland and the US while also reflecting the Irish perspective on wider global affairs. The minister said the aim within Government is to continue to deepen the relationship between Ireland and the US in the period ahead. Just weeks out from the 6 October Budget Mr Chambers insisted that no decision has yet been taken on future carbon tax increases and the matter remains under review. But he stated that the Government is conscious of the rising energy costs facing households. He indicated that there would be a substantial income tax package in the Budget but added that it would be moderate overall.

stories.title: Taoiseach accepts high corporate tax proportion a concern
stories.summary: The Taoiseach has said he accepts that the proportion of taxation coming from corporation tax is a concern. Micheál Martin was speaking after Exchequer returns yesterday revealed that corporation tax had risen again in August, up by one third on the same time last year to €2.8 billion. "Parallel with that, our public expenditure has grown very, very significantly since 2020, particularly the onset of Covid and the unprecedented interventions we've made, so it's at a higher plateau now, public expenditure, than it would have been prior to that era," he said. Mr Martin said it was important that some of the corporation tax was aside for the Government's Future Ireland Fund, to deal with Ireland’s ageing population and increasing healthcare costs. He said some of the corporation tax take is also being used to deliver large scale infrastructure projects. "What I would say to balance the fact that we are, yes, depending - overly dependent - on corporation tax revenues, we are using it for the productive sector, so it's the productive capacity of the economy," Mr Martin said.

stories.summary: Jaguar Land Rover said today it would cut around 4,000 jobs globally over the next two years as part of a broader plan to reduce costs and improve competitiveness. stories.title: Iran says it will declare 'prohibited zone' near Strait
stories.summary: Iran's top security chief Mohsen Rezaei said his country would establish a "prohibited zone" near the strategic Strait of Hormuz, state media reported. "In the coming days, a prohibited zone will be announced outside the Strait of Hormuz. This zone will start from the US Navy's blockade line and include areas of the Persian Gulf. Any ship entering this new zone will be placed on the sanctions list" of Iran, Mr Rezaei told the state TV. Iran said its forces attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, hours after targeting ships in retaliation for American strikes on three oil tankers. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said the US should understand that the rules of the game in war against Iran have changed "before it is too late". "From now on, any attack against Iran's interests and security will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response," he said in a speech published on his Telegram channel. The latest round of clashes, which began with US raids last week, comes amid a deadlock in their six-month war.

stories.title: Grehan savouring the pinnacle of his golfing career
stories.summary: Stuart Grehan says Great Britain and Ireland's comeback victory to land the Walker Cup on Irish soil trumps anything he has achieved in the sport. The 33-year-old played an instrumental part in downing the United States at Lahinch golf club, turning over a three-point deficit before the final singles session after being wiped out in the morning foursomes to succeed 13.5 to 12.5. Grehan again leading the way against the world's number one amateur Preston Stout. The Offaly man came from two down with three to play to beat the Texan on Saturday, while on Sunday’s singles he was two down after the opening two holes before again getting the better of his illustrious opponent. In June Grehan captured the attention with victory in the Amateur Championship at Royal Liverpool, earning exemptions into this year’s Open Championship, as well as the 2027 Masters and US Open. "It’s 100% the best moment of my golfing career, by a long stretch," he said. "All the individual titles are fantastic, but this is history. We’re only the 10th team (Great Britain and Ireland) ever to win the Walker Cup, it’s an amazing moment."

stories.title: Joyce exit brings down curtain on colourful era
stories.summary: Padraic Joyce's departure brings to an end a colourful and tumultuous era in Galway football. A vibrant presence in the managerial paddock has exited stage left. Those pristine white runners will no longer traipse the inter-county sideline. The airpods have gone back in the case. The media will miss his occasionally unpredictable bluntness and his penchant for issuing cutting verdicts on his star players' performances. Rumours had swirled around social media in the week leading up to the All-Ireland final that Joyce was about to quit. On this desk, inquiries were made about whether we needed to have a 'Joyce departs...' article prepared and ready to go. Public denials were issued. There were, it has to be said, plenty of Galway supporters who wanted him gone in the wake of their sickening quarter-final defeat to Dublin. From our own sampling of the mood at the time, it's doubtful whether he would have survived a plebiscite within the county that week. But it appeared for all the world he was set on digging in and remaining at the helm. He was going to manage Galway to Sam or die trying.

stories.title: Round up: Ulster and Connacht bag first pre-season wins
stories.summary: Ulster and Connacht recorded their first pre-season victories in two tense tussles over the weekend. On Friday night, Richie Murphy's Ulster scraped past fellow URC challengers Edinburgh in Scotland, three weeks prior to their opening league clash on 25 September. As for Connacht, they were big winners over English CHAMP side Ealing Trailfinders, who's squad featured four Irish players. Ulster got their pre-season campaign off to an ideal start with a narrow two-point victory over Edinburgh in the Hive Stadium on Friday night. Debutant half-backs Jamie Benson and Matthew Devine combined for 11 points, with the former Connacht man scoring a first-half try, as Ulster raced into a 14 point lead after just 25 minutes. With a 27-man travelling squad named by Richie Murphy, all eyes were on the plentiful supply of new faces. Benson and Devine combined at half-back, Daniel Hawkshaw and Chay Mullins also started in the backline with Eduardo Bello, Ben Donnell, Eli Snyman and Martin Moloney all among the replacements. Academy prospects Flynn Longstaff and Jed Findlay rounded off the debutants from the bench also. The visitors raced into an early lead helped by set-piece dominance. A scrum penalty win led to the first try, with hooker James McCormick dotting down from the back of a powerful rolling maul. Edinburgh responded with a try of their own courtesy of centre Geordie Gwynn, but then came Ulster's gear change.

stories.title: Dublin Book Festival announces 20th anniversary programme
stories.summary: Dublin Book Festival has announced its 20th anniversary programme, with more than 120 events taking place across the capital from 4 to 8 November. The annual literary gathering will bring together established and emerging Irish writers, publishers, illustrators and readers for five days of talks, conversations, performances, book launches, workshops and family events. Among the names appearing this year are former president Mary Robinson, authors Roddy Doyle, Anne Enright, Marian Keyes, Sebastian Barry, Djamel White, Louise Kennedy and Jodi Picoult, as well as illustrator Oliver Jeffers, broadcaster Mario Rosenstock and writer and broadcaster Hector Ó hEochagáin. The festival will open with The Irish Times Women’s Podcast Book Club, with Róisín Ingle in conversation with Louise Kennedy, Sue Rainsford, Jan Carson and Sheila Armstrong. Other events will focus on subjects including climate change, censorship, nature, identity, Irish-language literature and the future of publishing. Mary Robinson will join Sadhbh O’Neill and John Gibbons for a discussion on books addressing the climate crisis, while she will also appear with rewilding writer Eoghan Daltun.

stories.title: Susan Sarandon 'still losing work over Palestine support'
stories.summary: Oscar winner Susan Sarandon has said she is still losing work ⁠because of her outspoken support for Palestinians, despite what she has described as a broader shift in public opinion against US support for Israel. Speaking at the Venice Film Festival on Sunday, where she is promoting her latest film The Echo Chamber, Sarandon said some parts of the film industry continue to shun her over her activism. "I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of the historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics," she said. "That has been a major revelation for people: how much money the United States gives to Israel. Nobody really understood that." Recent US opinion polls have shown support for Israel softening ‌and sympathy for Palestinians rising since ⁠the start of the Gaza war in 2023. However, 79-year-old Sarandon said her support for the Palestinian cause continues to carry professional consequences.

stories.title: Conor Pope's tips for saving money at home this winter
stories.summary: "Generally speaking, winter is very expensive," says Pope, explaining that heating and lighting our homes in the colder, darker months adds up. Additionally, the need to tumble dry clothes can be a big expense, alongside buying warmer clothing, extra food, and saving up for Christmas presents. "I've done the maths, and I reckon that winter time costs about €10,000 more for the average household than summer time," he states. "That's not even being wildly extravagant." The first step in bringing those costs down? Shopping around for an electricity provider. "The reality is that more than 70% of Irish consumers don't switch their energy provider," the savvy saver explains, "despite the fact that, even in a climate of rising prices, you can still knock about €500 off your annual bill - just by moving from company A to company B." Many people will avoid switching because it feels like too much hassle, but Pope insists that sites like Bonkers.ie and Switcher.ie make it incredibly straightforward.

stories.summary: A two-year-old boy has died in hospital after being struck by a car in Rathkeale, Co Limerick. The incident happened in the Abbeycourt area of the town this afternoon. He was taken by a family member to University Hospital Limerick (UHL) for treatment of serious injuries, where he was subsequently pronounced dead. A man in his 30s was arrested at a different location under suspicion of driving under the influence of an intoxicant. He was questioned at a garda station in Limerick and has been released, pending analysis of an evidential sample. A post-mortem examination will be conducted at UHL by the State Pathologist tomorrow.

stories.title: New helmet and high-vis e-scooter regulations in effect
stories.summary: New regulations requiring e-scooter users to wear helmets and high-visibility clothing have come into effect from today. Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien said yesterday that a ban on the use of e-scooters by under 18s could now be introduced by the end of this month or early next month, after he received permission from Europe to proceed with the plans. Mr O'Brien said he is now aiming to increase the minimum age for e-scooter use from 16 to 18 by late September or early October. Over the summer, the Government moved to change the regulations around e-scooters after medics at CHI Temple Street called for an outright ban on their use after six children ended up on life support in one fortnight due to injuries they sustained from e-scooters, using half of the hospital's ICU capacity. A ban for under 18s was announced, but the State was advised it needed to wait until later this year due to European rules. But yesterday, Mr O'Brien was told Europe has waived the waiting period.

stories.title: Euro zone economic growth revised up to 0.6%
stories.summary: The euro zone economy grew more than expected in the second quarter of 2026, according to revised data published today. The EU's statistics agency said GDP in the 21-country euro zone expanded by 0.6% between April and June, up from the 0.4% previously estimated. The revision was due to Ireland recording growth of 10.2% in the second quarter, well above the July estimate of 3.9%. Figures from the Central Statistics Office last week showed that Ireland's domestic economy fell 0.8% quarter-on-quarter from April to June, though growth for the previous three months was revised higher, while the more volatile gross domestic product rose 10.2%. With Ireland's large multinational sector often distorting GDP, officials prefer to use modified domestic demand (MDD) to gauge the strength of the economy. MDD growth for the first quarter was revised up to 1.7% from 0.3%.

stories.title: Is Russia's alleged hybrid war on EU a genuine threat?
stories.summary: This week Germany accused Russia of involvement in a drone attack on Leipzig-Halle Airport, marking a new low in relations between the two countries since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The charge, which Russia denies, casts a spotlight once again on the notion of an escalating 'hybrid' war being waged by Russia against EU countries supporting Ukraine. Is this a genuine threat, and if so, what has been Europe’s response? Russia’s alleged hybrid warfare directed at Europe reached an inflection point this week when Germany formally accused Moscow of an attempted drone attack on Leipzig-Halle Airport on 4 August. "The means used," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt declared on Tuesday, "such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems, are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine". There were three drones in all: one, filled with military grade explosives, was discovered by an alert bus driver next to a Ukrainian cargo plane; a second collided with a cargo plane in flight; and a third with traces of explosives was found in a nearby field.

stories.title: Arteta 'enjoyed every minute' of 'beautiful' comeback
stories.summary: Mikel Arteta hailed a "beautiful" win after Arsenal came from behind to beat Chelsea 2-1 at the Emirates Stadium. The Premier League champions required a response after conceding for the first time this season, Morgan Rogers stunning home fans into silence with a volleyed goal after 77 seconds before the hosts hit back against a Chelsea side still finding its feet under Xabi Alonso. Kai Havertz netted for the third time against his old club to equalise midway through the first half – a near-post effort that perhaps ought to have been kept out by Emiliano Martinez – then produced a sumptuous dummy to clear Martin Odegaard's path to goal, with the captain lashing home the winner in the 50th minute. "I think it was an exceptional performance," said Arteta. "I enjoyed every minute of it, from the beginning to the end. The beginning was tough but I enjoyed it because the team reacted in a spectacular way. The determination, the quality. It was beautiful. It was a fascinating game for the spectator. "I think it’s an indication for us of how capable we are to perform at an even higher level than last season. We still have a lot to grow and a lot to offer." The game marked another promising step back towards his best for Odegaard. His goal to win the game was reminiscent of his clever finish in the Community Shield against Manchester City, this time combining brilliantly with Havertz whose cunning step-over caught Chelsea’s defence flatfooted.

stories.title: Kildare's Rattigan embracing football's new era
stories.summary: After playing a full season of inter-county football under the LGFA's new playing rule enhancements, Aoife Rattigan is enjoying doing the same with her club Cappagh as they work their way through the highly-competitive Kildare intermediate football championship. Having initially trialled them during the Lidl National Football League and the Higher Education colleges competitions, the LGFA fully approved 12 new rules for their games at a Special Congress in April of this year. Whereas six of these regulations mirror the changes brought into the men’s game – such as the two-point scoring arc, the 'three up’ rule and the ‘solo and go’ – the rest were focused more so on the current rules of the LGFA. Rattigan thoroughly enjoyed playing under these new rules for the Lilywhites and continued to embrace them by kicking no fewer than three two-pointers in Cappagh’s opening round intermediate group stage win at home to Confey on 11 August. Although Cappagh as a team weren't as familiar with the rule enhancements as those who had been operating on the inter-county scene, Rattigan believes her club colleagues have quickly come to terms with the way the game is now being played. "I loved playing the new rules all year with Kildare, but at the start it took us a while to get used to them," she said.

stories.summary: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick insisted his side's start to the season was "not that bad" despite Everton’s added-time equaliser leaving them with just four points from three matches. Despite twice taking the lead through Bryan Mbeumo and Benjamin Sesko, United were pegged back by maiden Everton goals for Tyrique George and deadline-day signing Ainsley Maitland-Niles, who scored in the sixth minute of added time to seal a 2-2 draw. While Carrick said he was "bitterly disappointed" with the result, he did not think their points return, which already puts them five points behind leaders Manchester City, was the worst start. "We haven’t started the season that bad. It’s not that bad, we’ve got that close to coming away with three points today; that’s football," he said. "There are moments we can deal with a bit better, but we’ll be fine. "We’re bitterly disappointed to be up in the position we were in the game twice, so close to the end.

stories.title: Refreshed Van der Flier ready for World Cup year
stories.summary: Leinster and Ireland flanker Josh van der Flier knows that nothing is won in early September, but that doesn't mean that the 2027 Rugby World Cup escapes the imagination ahead of the start of the 2026/27 season. Speaking at the launch of the IRFU’s new men’s and women’s national team jerseys at the Guinness Open Gate Brewery this week, the 33-year-old was in fine form, which could be attributed to a healthy body and mind. "(I’m) feeling fit as well and getting back into a bit of pre-season stuff and ready for a big few months." This optimistic outlook will come as soothing words to head coach Andy Farrell, who prepares his 12-month plan where all roads hopefully lead to a World Cup final in Sydney on Saturday, 13 November. Van der Flier was part of the two most recent touring squads to Japan in 2019 and France in 2023, where both Irish efforts were ended by the All Blacks. There is a feeling of now or never ahead of the next edition however, but van der Flier insists that he is taking the coming months one at a time. "It's always tempting to start thinking of those (major tournaments), but it's obviously like how rugby goes, it tends to be week-to-week and you've got to look after your pre-season first," he said.

stories.title: 100 Buildings: Machine House - Ardnacrusha's iconic Power Station
stories.summary: One of the first major infrastructure projects for the Free State was the Shannon hydroelectric power station at Ardnacrusha, Co. Clare. It involved the construction of a huge dam and a power station, the scale of which had never been seen before, to harness the waters of the River Shannon to power a national electric grid. This far-seeing civil engineering project would eventually enable the rural electrification of Ireland. The idea of the Shannon Scheme was the brainchild of a young Irish engineer, Dr Thomas A. McLaughlin (1896-1971), who had worked as a graduate for Siemens-Schucker in Berlin in 1922 (1). He returned to Ireland the following year with a proposal for Siemens to implement this electricity expansion to the Irish government. His Shannon Scheme was more productive and cost-effective than the Dublin-centred plan, based on the River Liffey, which was then being considered (2). The contract for the construction work was awarded to Siemens in 1925. The power station had, as Seán Rotherty writes, a 'truly Germanic look' in its utility with its high-pitched roof with tiny dormer windows in its double attic. The large steel-framed and concrete-walled power station has an impressive industrial look devoid of ornamentation. It is a monumental complex of transformer rooms, control rooms, switch houses and cooling houses but they are interconnected to give the streamlined appearance of a single building. The dam/sluice house to the rear of the power station has a flat roof with a T-shaped plan. The power station is a protected structure on the Clare County Council Development Plan (RPS No. 311). The Electricity Supply Board (ESB) was created to manage the new station in 1927 with Dr Thomas A. McLaughlin appointed as its first managing director. The Shannon Scheme was operational in 19293, producing almost all of Ireland’s electricity needs. It was one of the largest hydroelectric stations in the world, creating 3,000 jobs and costing about 20 per cent of the government expenditure. The Shannon Scheme formally opened on 22 July 1929. The legacy of the German engineering at Ardnacrusha is present today with the standard electric voltage in Ireland at 220 volts following the German system, as opposed to 240 volts in the UK (4). The Shannon power station continues to produce electricity but its output is today only a tiny percentage of the national electricity production. It changed the Irish landscape physically with substations and generators as well as poles, pylons and wires, metaphorically bringing modernity and ambition to the fledging Free State. Thank you to photographer John Glynn for his generous use of his photographs and to Dermot Finnan of ESB. Read more entries from the 100 Buildings series here.

stories.title: Rob Reiner wins posthumous Emmy Award
stories.summary: Rob Reiner has been posthumously honoured with an Emmy Award for his guest appearance in the series The Bear. The Spinal Tap director, 78, and his wife Michele Singer Reiner, 70, were found dead from apparent stab wounds in their home in Los Angeles last December. Their son Nick, 32, has been charged with two counts of first-degree murder. He has pleaded not guilty. On Sunday night in the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, Reiner was announced as one of the winners at the ceremony formerly known as the Creative Arts Emmys. He won the award for Outstanding Guest Actor in a Comedy Series after playing Albert Schnurr on a 2025 episode of The Bear. Following the announcement of his win, presenter Wendi McLendon-Covey told the audience it was "appropriate to stand for this one".

stories.title: Presidential talks wedged within Trump's golf appearance
stories.summary: Unlike US presidents who came before him, Donald Trump's visit to Ireland this week is about the fairways, rather than searching for roots. While it is unlikely he'll pose with a pint of the black stuff in an ancestral home like Barack Obama or Ronald Reagan, or name a family pet after a village in Ireland (Richard Nixon had an Irish setter called King Timahoe), Mr Trump will be welcomed by hundreds of locals and tens of thousands of golf fans at the Amgen Irish Open at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg. Much of his weekend will be spent at the event in West Clare, where it is expected he will present the trophy to the Irish Open winner on Sunday. But just because the avid golfer has limited political engagements, with the trip being personal rather than an official state visit, doesn’t mean it will be a quiet or unassuming affair. After teasing the visit for months, President Trump is expected to land in Dublin on Saturday morning aboard his new Air Force One, the aircraft given to him by Qatar, and he will be greeted by Tánaiste Simon Harris. The Phoenix Park is set to become something of a political fortress, with a high-security operation in place by the end of the week, as Mr Trump starts his weekend with a visit to Deerfield Residence, the official residence of the US Ambassador to Ireland.

stories.title: Life of Irish folk musician Barry honoured in Co Down
stories.summary: Musicians, including members of the Traveller community, have gathered to commemorate an Irish folk musician cited as an influence by singers like Bob Dylan and Luke Kelly of the Dubliners. Margaret Barry was a singer and banjo player who was prominent on the international folk scene in the 1950s and 1960s. She left home at 15 with just her banjo and a bicycle to follow her love of music. It took her to some of the world's biggest venues, including Carnegie Hall in New York and the Newport Folk Festival in Rhode Island where she played on the same bill as Joan Baez and Bob Dylan. While not born into a Traveller family, she later met a Traveller, embraced the life and promoted the culture. She eventually settled in the small Co Down village of Laurencetown where she was buried after her death in 1989.

stories.title: Russian manner over Leipzig incident 'outrageous' - Byrne
stories.summary: The Minister for European Affairs has said that what Russia was doing was "absolutely outrageous" following an attempted drone attack in Leipzig in Germany last month. Allies rallied around Germany after it blamed the incident at Leipzig/Halle airport on Russia. Yesterday, the Department of Foreign Affairs summoned the Russian ambassador in response to the attempted attack. In a statement, the Russian Embassy said the Irish side "repeated insinuations by the German government" regarding the alleged attempted drone attack. It said Ambassador Yuriy Filatov "categorically rejected allegations of a Russian connection to the incident", adding that any claims of Russian involvement in any hybrid activities in Europe are "absolutely unfounded and misplaced". Minister Thomas Byrne said that his sympathy and empathy went to the Ukrainian people, and that he paid no attention to what Mr Filatov said. "Neither does anybody here in Ireland," he said.

stories.title: Another rate hike - for insurance: 5 questions for ECB
stories.summary: The European Central Bank is widely expected to hike interest rates on Thursday, erring on the side of caution as the US-Iran wardrags on, keeping oil prices high and raising inflation again. Brent crude has risen over the last month, while European gas prices have hit their highest since early 2023. Yes, basically. Sources told Reuters the ECB is ready to raise rates again in September, echoing the minutes of the July meeting. Traders have fully priced in a quarter-point move to 2.5% as the latest data shows euro zone inflation rose back above 3% in August on higher energy costs. "We expect the ECB to hike rates by 25 basis points. Another insurance rate hike," said ING's global head of macro Carsten Brzeski. "Or for those who don't like this term: a dovish rate hike." Policymakers have little appetite to signal further rate increases.

stories.title: Kremlin says Ukraine talks with US envoys were 'useful'
stories.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of "highly useful" talks with two US envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough. The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner "outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement." Mr Ushakov did not say what these ideas were. He said Mr Putin had told the pair that Russia was making "real progress" on the battlefield, was confident of achieving its goals, and stressed the necessity of addressing "all the root causes of the conflict." All these are statements that Russia has made repeatedly in the course of the war, which has dragged on for more than four and a half years and has seen both sides intensify long-range air strikes in recent weeks while the front lines remain largely static. There was no comment from Mr Witkoff and Mr Kushner, who were visiting Russia for the first time since January on behalf of US President Donald Trump. They flew out of Russia soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv today.

stories.title: Grehan sinks Stout as GB&I triumph in Walker Cup thriller
stories.summary: Great Britain & Ireland won the Walker Cup for the first time in 11 years in sensationally dramatic fashion in Lahinch - with Josh Hill sinking a four footer on the 18th to seal a 1up win over Tyler Watts and deliver a 13.5 to 12.5 victory for the hosts. Trailing by three points before the final singles session after being wiped out in the morning foursomes, the GB&I team seized the initiative in the early singles matches, with Ireland's Stuart Grehan again leading the way against the world's number one amateur Preston Stout. Amateur champion Grehan, who'd come from two down with three to play to beat Stout on Saturday, had gotten off to a wretched start on Sunday, shanking his bunker shot on the first to lose the opening hole. Stout birdied the second to go 2up but as the wind picked up and the weather worsened, Grehan gained the upper hand, winning the fifth and sixth holes to go all square. The Offaly man seized the initaitive early on the back nine, stitching his second shot to a few feet on the par-five for a gimme eagle to go 1up for the first time. He won the next two holes against a faltering Stout to take a three hole lead. While Stout rallied to win the 15th, Grehan held firm to win 2&1. It capped off a memorable weekend for the 33-year old former pro, Grehan, who had taken 2.5 points from four matches, winning both his singles matches at the top of the order.
